issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may set aside an acquittal when a proper assessment of the evidence supports guilt and the trial court’s rejection of the evidence overlooked material features.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted all accused after treating the evidence concerning two incidents as generally unreliable.
The injured victim gave an account identifying the six appellants, and an earlier recorded statement substantially corroborated his testimony.
A co-sharer who accompanied the victim to the garden also supported the account of the assault.
The High Court separated the unreliable evidence concerning the later incident from the evidence concerning the first incident and considered the victim’s injuries and corroborated account.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in interfering with the acquittal of the six appellants in relation to the assault on the victim.
issues.legal_principle: An acquittal may be reversed where the evidence, properly sifted, supports the finding of guilt; here, the victim’s testimony was supported by the corroborating recorded statement and an eyewitness, and the trial court had overlooked material features. The judgment cites no earlier case or particular provision for this principle.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquittal and victim_identifies_assailants and victim_account_is_corroborated and trial_court_overlooks_material_evidence

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The case is an appeal seeking to overturn an acquittal.
predicates.victim_identifies_assailants: The injured victim identifies the persons who committed the assault.
predicates.victim_account_is_corroborated: Other evidence, such as a prior recorded statement or an eyewitness, supports the victim’s account.
predicates.trial_court_overlooks_material_evidence: The trial court rejects the evidence without properly considering material evidence bearing on the incident.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, the victim identifies the assailants, the victim’s account is corroborated, and the trial court overlooks material evidence, appellate interference with the acquittal is justified.

issues.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapons are liable for rioting while armed when the evidence establishes their participation in the assembly and assault.
material_facts: The six appellants were found to have participated in an unlawful assembly formed to assault the victim.
They were armed with deadly weapons when the assault occurred.
issues.conclusion: The convictions of the six appellants for rioting while armed with deadly weapons were justified.
issues.legal_principle: Section 148 of the Indian Penal Code applies to rioting while armed with a deadly weapon or an object which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death. The court upheld the convictions under that provision; it noted that liability under Section 149 could have been applied to the assault offence, but that the High Court had not done so.

predicates.unlawful_assembly_proceeding: The case concerns alleged participation in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.accused_participated_in_unlawful_assembl: The accused participated in an assembly with an unlawful common object.
predicates.accused_was_armed_with_deadly_weapon: The accused was armed with a deadly weapon or an object likely to cause death when used as a weapon of offence.

issues.definition: In a case concerning an unlawful assembly, participation in the assembly while armed with a deadly weapon supports an armed-rioting conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for attempted murder must be reduced where a grievous, life-endangering injury does not establish an intention to cause death, while the evidence supports grievous hurt by a dangerous weapon.
material_facts: The appellant thrust a spear into the victim’s chest, causing a grievous wound that endangered the victim’s life.
The other three recorded injuries were simple, and the court found that the chest injury was not shown to be one that would necessarily have caused death without timely medical aid.
The evidence therefore did not establish the intention to cause death required to sustain the attempted-murder conviction.
issues.conclusion: The attempted-murder conviction was replaced with a conviction for grievous hurt by a dangerous weapon, and the sentence was reduced from five years to three years of rigorous imprisonment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code requires the intent or knowledge specified for an attempt to murder. On these facts, that intent was not established beyond doubt; the grievous injury caused by the spear instead supported conviction under Section 326 IPC.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_attempted_murder_co: The case is a criminal appeal challenging an attempted-murder conviction.
predicates.grievous_injury_caused_by_dangerous_weap: The accused caused grievous hurt using a dangerous weapon.
predicates.death_intent_not_established: The evidence does not establish an intention or knowledge sufficient to support an attempted-murder conviction.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an attempted-murder conviction, the accused caused grievous hurt with a dangerous weapon, and the evidence does not establish the required intent or knowledge concerning death, the conviction is for grievous hurt by a dangerous weapon.

issues.legal_issue: An assault causing simple hurt with a weapon likely to cause death when used as a weapon of offence supports conviction for voluntarily causing hurt by a dangerous weapon rather than attempted murder.
material_facts: The appellant struck the victim on the head with a farasa.
The resulting scalp wound was classified as a simple injury.
The court found that the weapon, used as a weapon of offence, was likely to cause death, but the injury did not support the attempted-murder conviction.
issues.conclusion: The attempted-murder conviction was replaced with a conviction for voluntarily causing hurt by a dangerous weapon, and the sentence was reduced from six years to two years of rigorous imprisonment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 324 of the Indian Penal Code applies to voluntarily causing hurt with an instrument which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death. The court applied that provision because the injury was simple but the weapon met that description; it did not cite an earlier case.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_attempted_murder_co: The case is a criminal appeal challenging an attempted-murder conviction.
predicates.simple_hurt_caused_by_dangerous_weapon: The accused caused simple hurt using an instrument that is dangerous when used as a weapon of offence.
predicates.weapon_used_as_weapon_likely_to_cause_de: The instrument, used as it was in the assault, was likely to cause death.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an attempted-murder conviction and the accused caused simple hurt with an instrument likely to cause death when used as a weapon, the conviction is for hurt with a dangerous weapon.

issues.legal_issue: Instigating an assault with deadly weapons, without sufficient proof that the instigation was to kill, supports conviction for abetting hurt with a dangerous weapon rather than abetting attempted murder.
material_facts: The appellant instigated the others to assault the victim, and the assault was carried out with deadly weapons.
The victim’s testimony described the instigation as an order to kill, but the earlier recorded statement described it as an order to assault.
The court treated the established instigation as one to assault with deadly weapons and did not find the more serious allegation sufficient to sustain abetment of attempted murder.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for abetting attempted murder was replaced with a conviction for abetting voluntarily causing hurt by a dangerous weapon; the two-year sentence was unchanged.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 324 and 109 of the Indian Penal Code apply to abetment of voluntarily causing hurt with an instrument used as a weapon of offence and likely to cause death. The conflicting accounts of the instigation supported the lesser offence rather than abetment of attempted murder. The judgment cites no earlier case.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_abetment_of_attempt: The case is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction for abetting attempted murder.
predicates.accused_instigated_assault_with_dangerou: The accused instigated an assault that was carried out with dangerous weapons.
predicates.instigation_to_kill_not_established: The evidence does not establish that the accused instigated the assailants to kill the victim.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a conviction for abetting attempted murder, the accused instigated an assault with dangerous weapons, and instigation to kill is not established, the conviction is for abetting hurt with a dangerous weapon.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for simple hurt need not be modified where the evidence supports the offence and no basis for changing the conviction or sentence is established.
material_facts: The appellant was convicted of simple hurt and sentenced to one year of rigorous imprisonment.
The Supreme Court found no reason to modify that conviction or sentence.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for simple hurt and the one-year sentence were left unchanged.
issues.legal_principle: Section 323 of the Indian Penal Code provides for punishment for voluntarily causing hurt. The court found no ground to alter the conviction or sentence under that provision and cited no earlier case.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_simple_hurt_: The case is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction for simple hurt.
predicates.evidence_supports_simple_hurt: The evidence supports that the accused voluntarily caused hurt.
predicates.no_basis_to_modify_conviction_or_sentenc: The court finds no reason to change the conviction or sentence.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a simple-hurt conviction, the evidence supports the offence, and there is no basis to change the conviction or sentence, both remain unchanged.

issues.legal_issue: A joint trial is not vitiated by misjoinder where connected offences formed part of one transaction and the joinder caused no prejudice to the accused.
material_facts: Several accused were tried together in relation to assaults occurring one after another.
The later assault was found to be an offshoot and consequence of the first assault, and some accused were common to the events.
The accused who were not present during the first incident were acquitted, and the appellants suffered no prejudice from the joint trial.
issues.conclusion: The trial was not vitiated by misjoinder of charges.
issues.legal_principle: Section 223 of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits persons to be charged and tried together in specified circumstances, including where offences are committed in the course of the same transaction. The court held that the incidents formed one transaction and that no prejudice resulted; it cited no earlier case.

predicates.joint_trial_for_connected_offences: The accused were tried together for offences connected with multiple events.
predicates.offences_form_part_of_one_transaction: The offences arose as parts or consequences of one connected transaction.
predicates.no_prejudice_to_accused: The joint trial caused no prejudice to the accused.

issues.definition: When connected offences are tried together, form part of one transaction, and the joint trial causes no prejudice to the accused, the trial is not vitiated by misjoinder.
